valley/budget: Fix a budget of one point two times ten to the twenty two FLOPs. Compute is six N D, so the bigger the model, the fewer tokens it can afford to read.
valley/sizes: Train models of many sizes on that same budget, and plot each one's final loss against its size.
valley/small: Too small, and the model lacks the room to learn, however many tokens it reads.
valley/big: Too big, and it reads too few tokens to train all those parameters: it is under-trained.
valley/best: The bottom of the valley is the compute-optimal size. Measured across many budgets, it sits at about twenty tokens per parameter.
solve/sub: Put D equals twenty N into C equals six N D. Six N times twenty N: C is a hundred and twenty N squared.
solve/root: So N is the square root of C over a hundred and twenty.
solve/divide: For our budget, write a hundred and twenty as one point two times ten squared. Divide the leading numbers: one point two over one point two is one. Divide the powers of ten by taking two from twenty two: ten to the twenty.
solve/billion: A billion is ten to the nine, and a billion times a billion is ten to the eighteen, since the powers add. So write N squared in billions squared: ten to the twenty is a hundred times ten to the eighteen.
solve/ex: Take the square root of each part: the root of a hundred is ten, and the root of ten to the eighteen is a billion. So N is ten billion parameters, trained on twenty times that: two hundred billion tokens.
solve/grow: N grows as the square root of C. So four times the budget buys twice the parameters and twice the tokens: they grow together.
ratio/ratio: To judge a trained model, divide its tokens by its parameters, and compare with twenty.
ratio/under: A hundred and seventy five billion parameters on three hundred billion tokens is under two per parameter: badly under-trained. A smaller model, on more tokens, would have reached a lower loss for the same compute.
ratio/opt: Seventy billion parameters on one point four trillion tokens is twenty per parameter: compute-optimal.
ratio/over: Eight billion on fifteen trillion is nearly two thousand per parameter, far past compute-optimal. That costs extra training, but every forward pass afterwards is cheaper, at two N FLOPs per token.
try/p1: Try one. The budget is four point eight times ten to the twenty two FLOPs. How many billion parameters should a compute-optimal model have?
try/d1: Divide by a hundred and twenty. Four point eight over one point two is four, and twenty two minus two leaves ten to the twenty. So N squared is four times ten to the twenty.
try/e1: In billions squared, ten to the twenty is a hundred times ten to the eighteen, so N squared is four hundred times ten to the eighteen.
try/r1: The root of four hundred is twenty, and the root of ten to the eighteen is a billion: twenty billion parameters.
try/p2: Now the budget is one point nine two times ten to the twenty three FLOPs. How many billion tokens should the model see?
try/d2: One point nine two over one point two is one point six, and twenty three minus two leaves ten to the twenty one.
try/e2: In billions squared, ten to the twenty one is a thousand times ten to the eighteen, so N squared is sixteen hundred times ten to the eighteen.
try/r2: The root of sixteen hundred is forty: forty billion parameters. At twenty tokens each, that is eight hundred billion tokens.
